ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a distribution map of isolines of the Earth's surface rotational linear velocity. On the left side, isolines of 840, 870, and 900 kilometers/hour are marked, and the values generally increase from north to south. The two points a and b are roughly located at the same horizontal position, that is, they have the same latitude; but the isoline near a protrudes northward, making the rotational linear velocity corresponding to point a greater than that of point b at the same latitude. Reasoning: The question stem has already stated that a and b have the same latitude, so latitude difference cannot explain the difference in linear velocity. The Earth's rotational linear velocity can be expressed as v=ω(R+h)cosφ. Under the condition that angular velocity ω and latitude φ are the same, the higher the altitude h, the farther from the Earth's axis, and the greater the linear velocity. Therefore, the reason why point a has a greater linear velocity is that point a has higher terrain.

Then use the text statement that their latitudes are the same. Since latitude is fixed, the normal latitudinal factor cannot explain the difference; by v = ω(R+h)cosφ, the point with greater elevation has greater rotational linear velocity. Therefore a must be higher in terrain, so a点地势高，自转线速度大.

claims.source: Under the condition that angular velocity ω and latitude φ are the same, the higher the elevation h, the farther it is from the Earth's axis and the greater the linear velocity.

claims.claim: The larger linear velocity at point a is because the terrain at point a is higher.
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: Therefore, the reason why point a has a relatively large linear velocity is that point a has relatively high terrain.
